Karnataka’s oral epics include Manteswamy, Male Madeshwara, Junjappa and Siri Paddana. Their repertoires belong to distinct communities and local traditions, rather than one uniform statewide practice.
Folk tales form part of Karnataka’s oral prose traditions, alongside legends and myths. Storytellers share these narratives in local languages and settings.
Gaadegalu are Kannada proverbs, recognised as a concise genre of folk literature. Their meaning depends on the situation in which people use them.
Ogatugalu, or riddles, are a recognised form of Kannada folk literature. A question or description invites listeners to discover a concealed answer.
Folk songs are part of Karnataka’s wider living heritage of music, performance and craft. Repertoires are sustained through the voices of communities and their local traditions.
Sobane songs belong to local ceremonial and ritual repertoires. Research in Hassan documents women’s sobane singing associated with Somana Kunita; meanings and practices vary between communities.
Tatvapada is a Kannada song tradition concerned with spiritual and philosophical reflection. Performances use relatable language to explore questions about life and belief.
Historical recordings include grinding songs from Belagavi and transplanting and harvest songs from Sullia. They document music within agricultural and household work.
Suggi Kunitha is associated with the Halakki Vokkaliga community of Uttara Kannada. The seasonal celebration is connected with Kamana Hunnime and the farming calendar.
Somana Kunitha is a ritual performance associated with village-deity worship in parts of southern Karnataka, including Mandya, Mysuru and Hassan.
Huli Vesha, also called Pili Nalike, is associated with coastal Karnataka. Troupes perform during Navaratri and other community festivals in towns including Mangaluru and Udupi.
Channapatna is known for lacquered wooden toys and decorative objects. Workshops in the town continue a craft associated with turning, shaping and finishing wood.

Kasuti is a hand-embroidery tradition associated with Karnataka, especially the Dharwad region. Geometric arrangements and motifs drawn from architecture, animals and everyday surroundings appear on textiles.
Bidriware is a decorative metalworking tradition associated with Bidar. Its identity comes from inlaid patterns set against a darkened metal surface.
Kinnal in Koppal district is known for wooden toys and religious figures. Craftspeople known as chitragaras use lightweight wood and build up the surface before painting.
